body: A woman of thirty is at her sister’s church for the first time in nine years, because it is easier than the conversation about why she would rather not. She is standing with her coat still on, reading the words off the screen a beat behind everybody else. Halfway through the third song the words change — up to then it has all been you, you are faithful, you have never failed, and now it is he. He has done great things. And her sister, on her left, who has been singing with her eyes shut for ten minutes, opens them and sings that line out into the room. Not at her. Just outward. Then it goes back to you, her sister closes her eyes again, and nobody mentions any of it in the car.
That pronoun did not slip. Something in the room changed direction for four bars and changed back, and almost nobody in it could have told you it had happened.

Watch the pronouns in almost any worship song and they move. You are faithful is addressed upward. He has done great things is addressed to whoever is standing next to you. Most songs cross between the two without announcing it, sometimes inside a single verse.

Paul puts both jobs in one sentence and does not appear to think them separable: teach and admonish one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord. Teaching one another, and singing to Him — not two activities in sequence but one act with two directions. It is worth noticing how odd that is, because nothing else works that way. Prayer goes up. Preaching goes across. Conversation goes back and forth. Singing is the only ordinary thing a congregation does in which the same breath is addressed to God and heard as instruction by the person on the next chair, and neither use gets in the way of the other.

That is not only a fact about church buildings. This dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air today, and every track on all of them carries the passage it stands on, attached to a permanent identifier rather than a title somebody could later edit.

That last detail is the expensive one, and it exists because of the sideways direction. If a song were only prayer, its content would be a matter between the singer and God, and sincerity would nearly be enough. But a song is also teaching, and teaching can be wrong. So what a track asserts about God must be checkable, and must stay attached to the recording wherever it turns up on the dial. Sing it to God and it is prayer. Sing it beside somebody and it is teaching. It is always doing both, and the second job is the one that has to survive an inspection.

The horizontal half has quietly gone missing from how people talk about worship. The default picture now is a private emotional transaction with the lights down — just me and God, eyes closed, the room deliberately dark so that the room stops existing. There is something real in that. But it has trained a generation to hear congregational singing as a thousand separate solos in one building, and once that is the assumption, what everybody is singing at each other stops feeling like anybody’s business. It becomes rude to ask whether the line is true, as it would be rude to correct somebody’s prayer.

So the band keeps the congregational registers on their own frequencies rather than blending everything into a single worship average. There are stations for covenant worship, where the songs are largely declarations about what God has promised and done, and stations that are almost entirely address, sung upward. Learn roughly where they sit and you can pick the direction you need on a given morning — a real distinction, not a marketing one.
Taste has very little to do with any of this. What is at stake is what gets installed while the tune plays.

Be fair to the purely vertical song first, because the Psalms are full of them and they do what nothing else does: they hand a person words to say to God when they have none of their own, which on some mornings is all that is needed. But a song made entirely of address has nothing for the person beside you to catch. It gives them your posture without your reasons. A congregation fed only on that ends up with great warmth towards God and little it can state about him — which is fine until somebody is ill, or asks a hard question, and there turns out to be nothing underneath the warmth that can be said out loud.
Nobody braces against a chorus. That is the whole of the opportunity and the whole of the danger.

Two brothers are painting the front room of their mother’s house, which is being sold, and they have got to the stage where the furniture is in the middle under a sheet and the light through the bare window is wrong. One is fifty-four and the other forty-nine, and they have not spent a whole day together in years. The radio is on the mantelpiece because one of them put it there and neither has changed it. Somewhere in the afternoon the older one starts singing along, under his breath and not all of the words. On the second chorus the younger one comes in underneath him, and they get through it, and then the song ends and they keep painting. They finish the wall about six.

Nothing was addressed to either of them. Each was singing to God in a room with somebody else in it, and the somebody else heard every word — the entire mechanism working as designed, with no meeting, no service and nobody leading.

The uncomfortable half of this has to be said plainly. If a song teaches, a bad song teaches too, under the same conditions — unexamined, at volume, forty times over. A station playing into a kitchen for eight hours is catechising everybody in it, including the ones who never agreed to be taught anything and would be annoyed to hear it put that way. That is real power in a small speaker on a windowsill, and it is not less real because the intentions behind it are good.

The answer is not to sing less, which is the response of somebody who has decided the medium is the problem. It is that whoever loads the songs onto the transmitter must say what each one stands on and let anybody check it. If nobody braces against a chorus, the only protection available is that the chorus is true — true in a way that can be pointed at, in a chapter, rather than merely felt by people who meant well. The lack of resistance is not a defect to be worked around. It is the format, and it is why the content has to be answerable.

So a worship song is never private, even when it is sung alone, and never only teaching, even when it is teaching hard. It goes up and it goes sideways in the same breath, and a station playing it into a room is quietly doing both to everyone there — the one with their eyes shut, and the one standing with their coat still on, reading the words a beat behind.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. No menu, no queue to build, nothing to decide before anything starts.

If you want somewhere to begin, begin at HM 303.10 — Yes and Amen. Its format is covenant worship, the clearest place on this dial to hear both directions at once: the songs there are largely statements about what God has promised and done, sung to him, and so heard as instruction by anybody in earshot who was only making the tea. Put it on and do what this article started with — listen to the pronouns. Count how often a song turns from you to he and back inside one verse. Once you have heard it you will not stop hearing it, in any song, in any building, for the rest of your life.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a lesson, which would rather spoil the point. Put HM 303.10 on this afternoon in a room where somebody else is doing something — a kitchen, a workshop, a front room with the furniture under a sheet. Do not explain it and do not ask them afterwards what they thought. Sing along if you sing. The other person will hear every word of it, and neither of you will have to say a thing about it.
